meta.blurb: When his brother has a heart attack, baker Walter realises he knows nothing about his own heart. Over six Thursday evenings, a cardiac nurse named Hana explains the pump, the pipes and the risks in plain words, and shows what small changes can do.
meta.bible: Walter: a baker of about fifty-eight, anxious at first, curious and kind. Karl: his older brother, who has a heart attack and recovers. Hana: a cardiac nurse who runs six free Thursday evening talks called Heart Talk at the Community centre. Her sister-in-law, the doctors and the pharmacist are minor characters. The story runs over about six weeks, from a cold Monday in the hospital to the last Thursday talk. Key terms: Heart, Atria, Ventricles, Valves, Coronary arteries, Arteries, Veins, Capillaries, Pulse, Blood pressure, Systolic, Diastolic, Hypertension, Cholesterol, Lipoproteins, LDL, HDL, Plaque, Atherosclerosis, Statins, Heart attack, Cardiac arrest, CPR, Defibrillator, Stroke, FAST, Heart failure, Arrhythmia, Atrial fibrillation, Sleep apnoea, Cardiac rehabilitation, Mediterranean, Diabetes, Aspirin, Millimetres, Mercury. Facts used, all general and hedged: an adult resting heart rate is usually 60 to 100 beats a minute, about 100,000 beats a day; about 120 over 80 is often called a healthy reading but targets vary; the World Health Organization suggests under 5 grams of salt a day; adults are commonly advised about 150 minutes of moderate activity a week; no single food or most supplements protect the heart; many researchers now doubt a daily glass of wine protects it; the long-term effects of vaping are still being studied. Voice: calm, plain and kind, a little humorous; science is real and hedged; no diagnosis and no personal medical advice. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: On a cold Monday morning, Walter gets a phone call from his sister-in-law. His brother Karl has had a heart attack, and Walter drives to the hospital with shaking hands.
Karl is awake and tired but smiling, and the doctors say that he is going to recover. Walter is relieved, yet he realises that he knows almost nothing about how the heart works.
In the corridor, a cardiac nurse named Hana notices Walter's worried face. She runs a free talk about the heart on Thursday evenings, and she invites him to come along.
At the first talk, Hana says that she can only give general information. For advice about their own health, she says, everyone should talk to their own doctor.
Hana holds up her fist and explains that the heart is about that size. It is a strong muscle, and its job is to pump blood around the body.
In an adult at rest, the heart usually beats between sixty and one hundred times a minute. That adds up to about one hundred thousand beats every day, without a single holiday.
Inside, the heart has four chambers, which are like small rooms. The two at the top are called atria, and the two stronger ones below are called ventricles.
Between the chambers are four valves, which work like doors that open in only one direction. The familiar lub-dub sound of the heartbeat comes from the valves closing.
The heart is really two pumps side by side. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen, and the left side sends it around the body.
Blood is the delivery service of the body. It carries oxygen and nutrients to every cell, and it carries waste products away so that they can be removed.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins bring it back. In between, tiny vessels called capillaries pass the oxygen to the cells.
Strangely, the heart cannot feed itself from the blood passing through its chambers. It has its own supply from the coronary arteries, which wrap around its outside like branches.
Hana asks everyone to place two fingers on the inside of the wrist, just below the thumb. The gentle tapping that they feel is the pulse, which is the heartbeat travelling along an artery.
On the second Thursday, Hana holds up a garden hose and turns on the tap. Blood pressure, she explains, is the force of the blood pushing against the walls of the arteries.
A blood pressure reading has two numbers, one above the other. The top number is measured when the heart beats, and the bottom number is measured when the heart rests between beats.

A reading of around one hundred and twenty over eighty is often described as healthy. However, targets differ between people and between countries, so only a doctor or nurse can say what a number means for you.
High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms at all, which is why it is often called a silent problem. The only way to find out is to have it measured with a cuff.
When pressure stays too high for years, it can damage the walls of the arteries. It also makes the heart work harder, and over time the muscle can become tired.
Too much salt can push blood pressure up in many people. The World Health Organization suggests less than five grams a day, and most of our salt comes from processed food, not the salt shaker.

On Friday, Walter visits the pharmacy and has his blood pressure checked, sitting still and quiet with his feet flat on the floor. The result is a little higher than he expected, so he books an appointment with his doctor.
On the third Thursday, Hana talks about cholesterol. It is a waxy, fatty substance, and the body needs some of it to build cells and make certain hormones.
Cholesterol travels around the blood in carriers called lipoproteins. LDL carries it out to the body and is often called the bad kind, while HDL helps to carry it back to the liver.
Over many years, fatty deposits called plaque can build up inside the walls of the arteries. The pipe becomes narrower and stiffer, and this slow process is known as atherosclerosis.
The liver makes most of the cholesterol in the body, so food is only part of the story. Diet matters, but so do genes, and some people have high cholesterol even when they eat very carefully.

A simple blood test can measure cholesterol, and a doctor decides what the numbers mean for each person. Some people are given medicines called statins, and they should never stop taking them without talking to their doctor.
Not all fats are the same. Fats in olive oil, nuts and oily fish are generally better for the heart than the saturated fats found in butter, cream and fatty meat.

In the fourth week, the room is very quiet, because Hana is going to talk about heart attacks. A heart attack happens when a coronary artery becomes blocked, and part of the heart muscle cannot get the blood that it needs.

The classic warning sign is a pressure or tightness in the middle of the chest. The feeling may spread to the arm, the jaw or the back, and it can come with breathlessness, a cold sweat or feeling sick.
Heart attacks do not always look like the dramatic scenes in films. Women, older people and people with diabetes may notice only tiredness, nausea, back or jaw pain or a feeling of breathlessness.
If you think that someone may be having a heart attack, call the emergency number at once. Do not drive yourself to the hospital, because the ambulance crew can start treatment on the way.
A cardiac arrest is not the same as a heart attack. In a cardiac arrest the heart suddenly stops pumping blood properly, and the person falls unconscious and does not breathe normally.
Hana kneels beside a training doll and shows how to press hard and fast in the centre of the chest. A machine called a defibrillator, found in many public places, will speak and tell you what to do.

A stroke is not the same as a heart attack, because it happens in the brain. The letters FAST help people to remember the signs: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty and Time to call for help.
Heart failure sounds frightening, but it does not mean that the heart has stopped. It means that the heart does not pump as well as it should, and there are medicines and treatments that help.

On the fifth Thursday, Hana writes the words risk factors on the whiteboard. These are things that make heart disease more likely, and she draws two columns, one for things we can change and one for things we cannot.
Nobody can change their age or their genes, and Walter feels a little gloomy at first. Hana reminds him that the first column is the longer one, and that even small changes in it can lower the risk.
Smoking is one of the biggest risks for the heart and the arteries. The benefits of stopping begin quickly, and doctors, pharmacists and help lines can all support people who want to quit.
Heavy drinking can raise blood pressure and can weaken the heart muscle over time. The old idea that a daily glass of wine protects the heart is now doubted by many researchers.

No single food saves the heart, but an overall pattern of eating can help. Diets rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish and olive oil are linked with a lower risk of heart disease.
Shops are full of superfoods and supplements that promise to protect the heart. For most vitamin pills there is no clear evidence that they do, so it is wise to ask a doctor before spending money.
In the sixth week, Hana asks the group to stand up and walk. Moving more helps the heart, and a common aim for adults is about one hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity every week.
Hana says that sleep is part of heart health too. People who regularly sleep too little seem to have a higher risk of heart problems, although researchers are still working out exactly how and why.

Long-term stress and loneliness are linked with a higher risk of heart problems, although scientists do not fully understand why. Friends, rest, laughter and time outdoors do not cure anything, but they can help us to cope.

Diabetes, a condition in which blood sugar stays too high, raises the risk of heart disease. Extra weight around the middle also raises the risk, and a doctor can help anyone who needs support with either.
Many people think that heart disease is mainly a problem for men, but it is a leading cause of death for women as well. A family history of heart problems at a young age is worth telling to a doctor.
Walter visits his own doctor for a health check. The doctor measures his blood pressure and sends him for blood tests, and Walter learns that it is useful to know his own numbers.
Karl joins a rehabilitation programme, where nurses and trainers help him to get stronger. It is normal to feel low or frightened after a heart attack, and he is told that he can talk about that too.
Hana ends with some common myths. Heart disease is not only for old people, feeling fine does not prove that all is well, and nobody should guess that chest pain is nothing.
Walter makes a small, realistic plan after talking it over with his own doctor. On the last Thursday he brings Karl to the talk, and the whole group claps for them both.
This book has given general information about the heart, and the science is still growing. It is not medical advice, so please talk to your own doctor or nurse about your own health.
C1C2: The telephone rang just after seven on a cold Monday morning, and Walter, who was kneading dough in his bakery, knew from his sister-in-law's voice that something was badly wrong. His brother Karl, only three years older than himself, had suffered a heart attack in the night and was now in the hospital. Walter wiped the flour from his hands, locked the shop and drove across town with a trembling grip on the wheel.

To Walter's great relief, Karl was awake, pale but smiling, and the doctors were confident that he would recover. Sitting beside the bed, listening to the quiet beeping of the monitor, Walter was struck by an uncomfortable thought: he had spent almost sixty years in the company of his own heart and could not have explained how it worked. If it could fail so suddenly in his brother, it could fail in him, and he wished above all else that he understood.

In the hospital corridor, a cardiac nurse named Hana noticed Walter's anxious face and stopped to ask whether she could help. She ran a free series of six Thursday evening talks at the community centre, she explained, in which she described the heart in plain words and answered every question people were too shy to ask elsewhere. Walter, who normally avoided meetings of any kind, found himself taking the leaflet and promising to come.

On the first Thursday, a dozen people sat on plastic chairs in the community hall while Hana wrote the words Heart Talk on the whiteboard. She began with an honest warning: what she was going to share was general information about hearts in general, and she could not tell anybody in the room what to do about their own. For that, she said firmly, they would need their own doctor, who knew their history and could examine them.

Hana began by closing her hand into a fist and holding it up for everyone to see, because a healthy adult heart is roughly that size. It is not a delicate symbol of love, she said, but a tough, hard-working muscle whose single job is to pump blood around the body. Walter looked at his own fist and felt, for the first time, a kind of respect for what lay beneath his ribs.

At rest, Hana told them, the heart of a healthy adult usually beats between sixty and one hundred times each minute, though fitter people often have slower rates. Added together, that makes something like one hundred thousand beats every day, and several billion over the course of a long life. It is an extraordinary record for any machine, and the heart manages it without a day off and without asking for thanks.

Hana drew a heart on the whiteboard and divided it into four rooms, which are called chambers. The two upper chambers, the atria, receive blood as it returns, while the two lower ones, the ventricles, have thicker walls because they have to push the blood out with real force. Together they work like a four-roomed house in which every room has a precise and necessary job.

To keep the blood flowing in the right direction, the heart contains four valves, each of which opens like a door that swings one way only. Hana invited everyone to place a hand on their chest and imagine them snapping shut in turn, because the well-known lub-dub of a heartbeat is the sound of those valves closing. A valve that leaks or sticks can make the heart work harder, she added, and doctors can often hear the difference through a stethoscope.

Hana explained that the heart is really two pumps lying side by side, each with its own task. The right side sends blood on a short journey to the lungs, where it collects oxygen, and the left side, which is the stronger of the two, sends that fresh blood on a long journey to the brain, the muscles and everything else. The blood then returns, tired and short of oxygen, and the circle begins again.

Blood, Hana said, is the delivery service of the body, and the heart is the engine that keeps its vans on the road. It carries oxygen from the lungs and nutrients from food to every single cell, and on the return journey it collects waste products to be removed by the lungs, liver and kidneys. If the deliveries slow down or stop, the cells soon begin to suffer, and the brain is among the first to complain.

The blood does not wander freely through the body, Hana explained, but travels through a vast network of tubes. Arteries carry it away from the heart under pressure, veins bring it back, and between the two lie capillaries so thin that red blood cells have to squeeze through them in single file. It is in these tiny vessels that oxygen and nutrients finally pass into the tissues, and Walter listened with a kind of astonished delight.

It seems strange, Hana remarked, but the heart cannot feed itself from the blood that flows through its own chambers, because its walls are too thick to absorb it. Instead it depends on a set of small vessels called the coronary arteries, which branch across its surface and bring oxygen to the muscle itself. These are the arteries that matter most in a heart attack, and Walter wrote their name on his notepad and underlined it twice.

At the end of the first evening, Hana asked everybody to lay two fingers on the inside of the wrist, just below the base of the thumb, and wait quietly. The soft tapping Walter felt there was his pulse, the wave of pressure sent along the arteries with every heartbeat, and he found it oddly moving to feel his own life ticking under his fingertips. Resting pulses vary from person to person, she reminded them, and a single reading tells you very little.

A week later, Hana arrived with a garden hose and a bucket, and with a look of deep satisfaction she turned on the tap. Blood pressure, she explained, is simply the force with which the blood pushes against the inside walls of the arteries, much as water pushes against the inside of a hose. Some pressure is essential, since without it the blood could not reach the brain, but pressure that is too high, year after year, begins to do harm.

Every blood pressure reading, Hana said, is written as two numbers, one above the other, and measured in units called millimetres of mercury. The top number, the systolic pressure, is the force when the heart squeezes, while the bottom one, the diastolic pressure, is the force when the heart relaxes for a moment between beats. When a nurse says that your pressure is one hundred and twenty over eighty, she is giving you both numbers at once.

A reading of around one hundred and twenty over eighty is often described as healthy, Hana said, but the ideal can differ with age, with other conditions and even between different national guidelines. A single high reading does not mean that someone has high blood pressure, because pressure rises with stress, coffee and even the walk to the clinic. That is why doctors usually want several readings, taken properly, before they say anything definite.

The trouble with high blood pressure, Hana warned, is that it usually causes no symptoms whatever, and a person can feel perfectly well for years while the pressure quietly does its damage. That is why it is sometimes called a silent condition, and why even people who feel fine are encouraged to have it measured from time to time. A cuff around the arm takes only a minute, and Walter promised himself that he would never again skip the test.

Pressure that stays too high for years, Hana explained, slowly wears out the walls of the arteries, making them stiffer and more likely to collect fatty deposits. It also forces the heart to push against greater resistance, so that the muscle thickens and may eventually grow tired, much like an engine that has been driven uphill for far too long. High blood pressure is among the leading risk factors for heart attacks, strokes and kidney disease.

Salt, Hana said, can raise blood pressure in many people, because the body holds on to extra water when there is too much sodium in the blood. The World Health Organization suggests that adults eat less than about five grams of salt a day, roughly a level teaspoon, yet most people eat far more because so much of it hides in bread, soups, sauces and processed meat. Herbs, lemon and spices, she added with a smile, can make food taste lively without it.

On Friday morning, Walter walked into the pharmacy, sat quietly for several minutes with his feet flat on the floor and his arm resting on the counter, and let the pharmacist wrap a cuff around his arm. The reading was a little higher than he had hoped, but the pharmacist explained that one measurement proves nothing and suggested that he mention it to his doctor. Walter booked an appointment at once, relieved to be doing something sensible instead of simply worrying.

In the third week, Hana turned to a word that everyone in the room had heard and few could explain: cholesterol. It is a waxy, fat-like substance that the body needs in order to build the walls of its cells and to make certain hormones, so it is not a poison, and she asked them to stop thinking of it as one. The trouble begins only when there is too much of the wrong kind travelling in the blood.

Because fat and water do not mix, cholesterol has to travel through the blood in tiny packages called lipoproteins, Hana said. The ones known as LDL deliver cholesterol to the tissues and are sometimes called the bad kind, because too much of them is linked with disease of the arteries, while HDL helps to carry cholesterol back to the liver and is called the good kind. The labels are a simplification, she admitted, but they are a useful way to remember which is which.

When the level of LDL cholesterol is high for many years, Hana explained, the walls of the arteries can gradually collect fatty deposits known as plaque. The passage narrows and stiffens, a slow process called atherosclerosis, much like a water pipe furred up with limescale. It usually begins silently, long before anything is felt, which is one reason why heart doctors talk so much about prevention.

Hana surprised many in the room by saying that the liver, not the dinner plate, produces most of the body's cholesterol. Food still matters, particularly foods rich in saturated fat and the artificial trans fats that are now banned or restricted in many countries, but genes matter too, and some people have high cholesterol however carefully they eat. It is therefore unfair, she said, to blame anyone for a high reading.

A simple blood test, Hana explained, measures the different kinds of cholesterol, but it is the doctor who decides what the numbers mean, after looking at the whole person, including age, blood pressure, smoking and family history. Many people are prescribed medicines such as statins to lower their cholesterol, and these have been studied in very large trials, though like all medicines they can have side effects. Anyone who is given such a medicine should ask their doctor any questions they have, and should never stop taking it without that conversation.

Fat, Hana said, is not the enemy, because the body needs some of it, but the type of fat makes a difference. Unsaturated fats, found in olive oil, nuts, seeds and oily fish, are generally kinder to the heart than the saturated fats in butter, cream, cheese and fatty meat, and when one replaces the other, cholesterol tends to improve. Nutrition science is full of arguments, she admitted, but on this point most experts broadly agree.

The fourth Thursday was the one Walter had been dreading, and the room was unusually quiet as Hana picked up her marker. A heart attack, she said, usually happens when a patch of plaque in a coronary artery cracks, and a blood clot forms on it and blocks the vessel, so that part of the heart muscle is suddenly cut off from its oxygen. Unless the blockage is cleared quickly, that muscle begins to die, which is why speed matters so much.

Hana listed the classic warning signs on the whiteboard, beginning with a pressure, squeezing or heaviness in the centre of the chest that lasts for more than a few minutes. The discomfort may spread to one or both arms, the neck, the jaw or the back, and it is often accompanied by breathlessness, a cold sweat, light-headedness or a wave of nausea. Walter copied the list carefully, thinking of Karl, who had at first mistaken the pain for bad indigestion.

Films, Hana said, have given us a false picture in which a man clutches his chest and falls to the floor, whereas in real life many heart attacks begin more quietly. Women, older people and people with diabetes are somewhat more likely to notice less typical signs, such as unusual tiredness, nausea, pain in the back or jaw, or simple breathlessness, and for that reason their symptoms are sometimes missed. If something feels seriously wrong, she urged, do not argue yourself out of it.

If you suspect a heart attack in yourself or in someone near you, Hana said, call the emergency number immediately and do not wait to see whether the feeling passes. It is much safer not to drive yourself to the hospital, because the ambulance crew can begin treatment on the way and can warn the hospital to be ready. Doctors have a saying that time is muscle, meaning that every minute of delay costs a little more of the heart.

Many people use the two terms as if they meant the same, Hana said, but a heart attack is a problem of blood supply while a cardiac arrest is a problem of electrical rhythm, in which the heart suddenly stops pumping effectively. The person collapses, becomes unconscious and does not breathe normally, and without help they will die within minutes. A heart attack can sometimes lead to a cardiac arrest, but it often does not, and a cardiac arrest can happen without any heart attack at all.

Hana knelt beside a training doll and showed the class how to do chest compressions, pressing hard and fast in the centre of the chest after calling for help. A machine called an automated defibrillator, found in many stations, shops and gyms, will switch on, speak to you and tell you exactly what to do, and it will not shock anyone who does not need it. A short first-aid course, she said, is one of the most useful things an ordinary person can ever learn, and she gave out the address of a local one.

A stroke, Hana went on, is a related but separate emergency, in which the blood supply to part of the brain is blocked or a vessel in the brain bursts. To help people recognise one, health services teach the letters FAST: a drooping Face, a weak Arm, slurred Speech, and the need to act at Time zero by calling the emergency number. Walter noticed that the same message, speed above everything, ran through every emergency she described.

The words heart failure, Hana said, frighten almost everyone, yet they describe a heart that is still working but pumping less strongly than the body needs, and many people live for years with good treatment. A different problem is an irregular rhythm, called an arrhythmia, of which atrial fibrillation is the most common, and the occasional flutter or skipped beat that most people notice is usually harmless. If it comes with dizziness, fainting, chest pain or breathlessness, however, a doctor should check it.

By the fifth Thursday the group had grown to nearly thirty, and Hana divided the whiteboard into two columns headed things you can change and things you cannot. In the second column she wrote age, being male, and a family history of early heart disease; in the first she listed smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, being inactive, carrying extra weight and heavy drinking. A risk factor is only a raised chance, she emphasised, and not a prediction about any one person.

Walter stared at the second column and felt a heaviness settle over him, since he could not alter his age, his brother or his family. Hana, noticing his expression, tapped the first column and pointed out that it was much longer, and that even modest changes in any of those items could lower the chance of trouble over the years. Nobody can control everything, she said, but almost everybody can influence something.

Of all the items in the first column, Hana said, smoking was the one that did the most harm, because it damages the lining of the arteries, makes the blood more likely to clot and raises the heart rate. The encouraging news is that the benefits of stopping begin within weeks and keep growing for years, and that doctors, pharmacists and telephone help lines can all support anyone who wants to try, even after several failed attempts. The long-term effects of vaping are still being studied, she added, so nobody should assume that it is simply safe.

Alcohol, Hana said, is a subject on which opinions have changed a great deal over the past few years. Heavy drinking is certainly harmful, since it raises blood pressure and can weaken the heart muscle, and the older belief that a daily glass of wine actively protects the heart is now doubted by many researchers, who suspect that earlier studies were misleading. If you choose to drink, she said, follow your country's guidance, and ask your doctor if you are not sure.

Hana was keen to stress that no single food rescues the heart, and that what counts is the overall pattern of eating over many years. Diets rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans, nuts, fish and olive oil, often called Mediterranean-style, have been linked with a lower risk of heart disease in many studies, and at least one large trial found a benefit too, though nutrition research is difficult and never perfectly clear. Fewer processed meats, sugary drinks and heavily salted snacks, she added, tend to point the same way.

Walking into any health shop, Hana observed, you would think that the heart could be saved by a berry, a powder or a bottle of capsules, but the research tells a more modest story. For most vitamin and mineral supplements, careful trials have not shown a clear benefit for preventing heart disease, and the evidence for fish oil capsules is mixed, so a varied diet is usually a better investment. A daily aspirin, she added, is a medicine that some people take on a doctor's advice, and healthy people should not start taking it on their own, since it can cause bleeding.

In the final week, Hana invited the whole group to leave their chairs and walk briskly around the hall, because the heart, she said, is a muscle that grows stronger with use. A common target for adults is about one hundred and fifty minutes of moderate activity a week, such as brisk walking, cycling or dancing, but even a little is better than nothing, and the benefits come from regularity rather than heroics. Anyone who has been inactive for years, or who has a health condition, should begin gently and talk to a doctor first.

Sleep, Hana said, is a part of heart health that is often forgotten, because the heart and blood vessels do much of their repair work while we rest. People who regularly sleep too little seem to have a higher risk of high blood pressure and heart disease, although researchers are still studying how much of the link is cause and how much is coincidence. Loud snoring with pauses in breathing, called sleep apnoea, can strain the heart, and anyone who suspects it should see a doctor.

It would be wrong to claim that stress alone causes heart disease, Hana said, but long-term stress and loneliness are both linked with a higher risk, partly because people under strain are more likely to smoke, drink, sleep badly and skip exercise. Scientists do not fully understand the whole picture, but it makes good sense to look after the mind as carefully as the arteries. Friendships, time outdoors and a laugh that makes your sides ache do not cure anything, yet they make the burdens lighter.

Two further risk factors, Hana said, often travel together: diabetes, in which the level of sugar in the blood stays too high and slowly damages the vessels, and carrying extra weight, especially around the middle of the body. Both raise the risk of heart disease, but neither is a moral failing, and both can often be improved with the right support, from healthy food and activity to medicine where a doctor recommends it. She asked people to be gentle with themselves, because shame, she noted, has never yet helped anyone lose weight.

A widespread myth, Hana explained, is that heart disease is a man's problem, whereas it is in fact one of the leading causes of death among women, who are sometimes diagnosed later because their symptoms can differ. She also encouraged everybody to find out whether close relatives had heart trouble at a young age, because some conditions run in families, and a doctor can take that into account. Walter, thinking of Karl, made a note to ask his own relatives some questions.

That week, Walter finally kept the appointment he had made, and his doctor measured his blood pressure properly, asked about his family and arranged blood tests for cholesterol and blood sugar. Knowing your own numbers, Hana had said, is like knowing the oil level in a car, because it lets you notice a change before it turns into a breakdown. Whatever the results turned out to be, Walter felt calmer simply for having asked the questions.

Karl, meanwhile, had been invited to join a cardiac rehabilitation programme, a supervised course of gentle exercise, advice about food and medicines, and encouragement, which research shows can help people recover and may lower the chance of another event. He told Walter that the hardest part had not been the exercise but the fear, and the nurses had reassured him that feeling low or anxious after a heart attack is very common. Talking about it, they said, was part of the treatment, not a sign of weakness.

Near the end of the course, Hana held up cards bearing the most common myths and crossed them out one by one. Heart disease is not only a problem for the old, since it can begin silently in middle age; feeling well does not prove that the arteries are healthy; and a natural remedy cannot cure a blocked artery, however enthusiastic the advertisement. Above all, she said, nobody should try to guess whether chest pain is indigestion or something serious, because the only safe answer comes from a professional.

By the end of the six weeks, Walter had made a plan that was small, realistic and agreed with his own doctor: a daily walk, less salt in the bread and the soup he sold, and a yearly check-up. On the final Thursday he brought Karl along, a little slower than before but cheerful, and the whole room applauded as the two brothers took their seats in the back row. Hana thanked them all for coming and told them that the best heart plan is the one that a person actually keeps.

As the lights went down in the community hall and the last chairs were stacked against the wall, Hana wished everyone good health and a long, full life. This book has offered only general information about the heart, and the research behind it continues to grow, so it is not medical advice and cannot replace a doctor or nurse who knows you. If you have chest pain, breathlessness or any worry about your heart, please contact a health professional or call the emergency number without delay.
